videoTitle: Prevent the Next Incident: AWS DevOps Agent Recommendations & SRE Chat
videoDescription:
The outage is fixed. Now make sure it never comes back. We rate the agent's investigation, run an on-demand evaluation, open the recommendation it writes about our own bug, switch on the fix it suggested, ask the agent a question in chat, and finish with a production checklist and a full, verified cleanup.

In this episode you will:
• Add feedback to the episode 3 investigation (Review tab: root cause correct + a note)
• Run a prevention evaluation now instead of waiting for the weekly run (Improvements · Run now)
• Read the recommendation: a pre-deploy memory load gate for the pipeline, naming our PR, commit and cache line, with next steps, trade-offs and alternatives
• Turn on the ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback, and see why the panel still says "Turned off" until a new deployment
• Ask the on-demand agent what changed in the last 3 hours and get a 5xx chart and the current error rate
• Walk through a production checklist and a multi-account reference architecture
• Delete everything on camera (Agent Space, EventBridge rule, API destination, connection, alarms, ECS service, ALB, target group) and prove it with the CLI

Cost: the evaluation took about 13 minutes of agent time (about $6 at $0.0083 per second); the chat about 4 minutes (about $2). Evaluations run weekly by default and use the same per-second price.

Accuracy notes: a deployment-configuration change alone starts no ECS deployment, so the Deployments tab keeps describing the previous deployment; force a new deployment to see "Circuit breaker: Monitoring". The circuit breaker came from the investigation's durable-fix note; the evaluation's recommendation targeted the pipeline.

videoTitle: EP 10 · Canary Deployment Explained: How One Update Crashed 8.5 Million PCs #Shorts
videoDescription:
EP 10 · One update. About 8.5 million Windows machines crashed. And it had passed validation.

On 19 July 2024, a faulty CrowdStrike content update (a config file, not new code) passed a validator that itself had a bug, and reached Windows PCs everywhere at the same time. Think of a wedding halwai who changes only the masala, gets a thumbs-up from a taster with a cold, and serves all 500 plates at once.

The interview answer: a metric-gated canary. Serve one table first, compare its error rate and latency with the old version, then widen 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%. Metrics worse? Automatic rollback, and only one table is hurt. And yes, config changes need canaries too.

Save this for your next system design round, and comment the deploy strategy your team uses.

videoTitle: Applying DevOps Where Assumptions Break | Borislav Sabotinov | DevOpsDays Austin 2026
videoDescription:
Applying DevOps Where Assumptions Break
Borislav Sabotinov, DevOpsDays Austin 2026 (Day 1, May 5, 2026)

High-Performance Compute (HPC) environments break many assumptions behind modern DevOps and CI/CD. Simulation jobs are long-running, stateful, and expensive to fail. Feedback can arrive hours or days too late to be useful.

This talk demonstrates how applying DevOps principles in an enterprise HPC and simulation environment saves valuable time by shifting focus away from deployments and toward feedback loops. From error troubleshooting after the fact to failure prevention. Instead of forcing standard CI/CD patterns  we adapted them to fit the constraints and delivered measurable value in reduced wasted compute, faster feedback, and better outcomes for engineers.

High-Performance Compute (HPC) environments are expensive to operate in part because a sizeable chunk of engineer and compute time is "wasted" via failed jobs. Engineers submit long-running jobs, wait hours or days, and only then discover failures or unusable results. By that point, the data is stale, decisions are delayed, and compute and engineer time is lost.

This talk is a real enterprise case study in applying a DevOps mindset to HPC by identifying and exploiting the true constraint: a reactive, instead of a proactive, feedback loop. We flipped the model from post-mortem analsysis to pre-submit validation and near real-time alerts so engineers could act with immediacy on timely, relevant data.

The result was a measurable decrease in wasted compute and faster recovery time. Hundreds of thousands of compute hours preserved, tens of thousands of engineer hours saved, and millions of dollars annually avoided in wasted reruns and idle decision time. 

This talk is about how applying DevOps principles to the actual constraint, not the visible symptoms, allowed value to flow all the way down to the customer in an environment where DevOps may not even be part of the conversation.

About Borislav Sabotinov:
Boris is a software engineer based in sunny Austin, TX working on large-scale engineering platforms that span High-Performance Compute (HPC), container orchestration platforms, and cloud systems. He cares about practical DevOps, improving feedback loops, and making complex systems less frustrating for the people who use them.

videoTitle: Git Merge vs Rebase
videoDescription:
Merge or rebase? Same code, different history.

Your feature branch has commits, and main moved on too. Here's how the two ways to bring them together actually differ.

🔀 git merge main ties the branches together with a merge commit. Nothing is rewritten.
📏 git rebase main replays your commits on top of main: one straight line, but brand-new commits with new IDs.
🤝 Rule of thumb: rebase your own branch before you push it; merge a shared branch others have pulled.

videoTitle: DevOps with Ansible Will Finally Make Sense After This

Ansible makes servers match a description you write once. We ran it for real on a small shop's three web servers: an inventory, ad-hoc commands, a first playbook that installs nginx and publishes the page, a second run that changes nothing (idempotence), a hand edit found with --check --diff and put right, the shell task that changes something every time, a handler that reloads nginx only when needed, and one variable that updates every server.

What we ran (ansible-core 2.16.3 on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS):

videoTitle: GitHub Actions Cache Miss? Fix It with restore-keys
videoDescription:
A GitHub Actions cache miss can still reuse a matching restore key. Build your exact key from the runner OS and a lockfile hash, then add broader restore-keys prefixes from most specific to least specific.

When a restore key matches, GitHub restores the newest matching cache. If the job succeeds, it saves a new cache under the exact key. Cache dependencies, never secrets.

Docs: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching

videoTitle: North Korea Robbed Binance Via A DevOps Laptop
videoDescription:
0:00 The Claude Code update that wasn't Anthropic's  
3:19 The checkout that took one cent  
4:49 Six billion dollars in twenty minutes

About $6.3 billion left Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, in roughly 20 minutes on October 29, the largest crypto theft on record. Binance points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop plus additional points of breach. TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute it to North Korea's TraderTraitor, the group behind the 2025 Bybit theft. About $2.7 billion in stablecoins was frozen; Binance says it will cover the losses. Kevin Beaumont says Binance uses Claude Code on Cursor, and the theft started inside the window when a backdoored Claude Code extension was live there; none of the companies has tied the two together.

Claude Code in Cursor: for about eleven hours on October 29, Cursor's extension marketplace served tampered versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) through Anthropic's official account there. A 66-line loader added an attacker's SSH key, tried to open a reverse SSH tunnel, set up persistence, and sent host details home. Bugs in the malware stopped the tunnel on most Mac and Windows machines, but the key and persistence stay even after you update. If you used Claude Code in Cursor that day, run Cursor's check for the svc-telemetry key and follow its remediation steps. Anthropic says its own systems weren't compromised; Cursor hasn't said how the upload happened.

Drupal: Commerce Core has an actively exploited access-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-118539) used to tamper with orders, including one-cent prices. Update to Commerce Core 3.3.13 or 8.x-2.41 and audit recent orders.

videoTitle: Helm vs Kustomize. Which Should You Use for Kubernetes Config?
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

Helm vs Kustomize, which should you use? Templating (Helm) vs overlay patching (Kustomize) for Kubernetes config, compared with the real helm and the real kubectl kustomize on one small chart.

THE IDEA

Helm is a package. A chart is a folder of templates full of blanks in double curly braces, plus a values file that fills them. Kustomize is a patch. It starts from ordinary Kubernetes files that already work and changes only what is different. One fills in blanks before the file exists, the other edits a file that is already finished.

THE CHART

My lab chart has 2 templates, 10 placeholders, and its templates read exactly 4 values. Hand that template straight to Kustomize and it refuses with a MalformedYAMLError, because it is not valid YAML until Helm renders it.

  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: {{ .Release.Name }}-web
  spec:
    replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}

PRODUCTION, THREE REPLICAS

Helm needed one line of values.

  replicaCount: 3

Kustomize needed 10 lines, a 4-line kustomization plus this 6-line patch. Same name, replicas, image and port either way.

  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: shop-web
  spec:
    replicas: 3

THE PROBLEM

I asked Helm for a node selector, a setting this chart never offered.

  $ helm template shop charts/web \
      --set nodeSelector.disktype=ssd

No error, no warning, and the output came out identical. Helm quietly ignored it. A chart can only change what its author left a blank for.

  exit 0
  warnings printed: 0
  output md5 without 314b0bf408
  output md5 with    314b0bf408
  nodeSelector in the output: no

ANY FIELD

Kustomize has no such limit. A patch can reach any field, because it edits the finished file.

  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: shop-web
  spec:
    template:
      spec:
        nodeSelector:
          disktype: ssd

BUT HELM KEEPS A HISTORY

Every install, upgrade or rollback adds a revision you can roll back to. Kustomize keeps no history at all. It just prints files.

USE BOTH

Many teams render the chart with Helm and then patch whatever the chart forgot with Kustomize. Helm's docs call this post rendering, a way to use tools like kustomize without the need to fork a public chart. I did exactly that.

  helm template -f values-production.yaml
  then kubectl kustomize on its output
  exit 0, objects 2
  replicas 3 (helm values)
  nodeSelector disktype: ssd (kustomize patch)
  patch: 9 lines, chart files edited: 0

ONE GOTCHA, MEASURED

Kustomize can also call Helm itself through its helmCharts field, but the Kustomize built into kubectl here (v5.7.1) could not run Helm 4. Kustomize v5.8.1 added Helm 4 support, so use a standalone kustomize that new, or render with helm first as above.

  kubectl kustomize --enable-helm
  exit 1
  objects rendered: 0
  error: unknown shorthand flag: 'c' in -c
  kustomize ran: helm version -c --short

WHEN TO USE WHICH

Someone else's software, take the chart. Your own app across environments, use Kustomize. A public chart that is missing one setting, render it with Helm and patch it with Kustomize.

Helm fills the blanks. Kustomize patches the rest.

videoTitle: How to Publish a Vibe-Coded Website? | Senior SWE Interview #0004
videoDescription:
You built a website with AI in one afternoon. The interviewer asks: "How would you publish it to production?"
A Senior answer: treat AI-written code like a pull request from a stranger, then ship it with a real pipeline.
🎯 Key points
1. Put it in Git and read every diff
2. Move secrets to environment variables, rotate any leaked key
3. Security review: server-side auth, input validation, database rules (RLS)
4. Pick hosting by app type: Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages or a managed backend
5. Custom domain, DNS records and free HTTPS
6. CI/CD with preview deploys and one-click rollback
7. Monitoring, error tracking and budget alerts
💡 Senior tip: the AI writes the code, but you own what goes to production.
💬 Interview follow-up: an API key was committed to a public repo. What do you do first? Answer in the comments 👇

videoTitle: Three Replicas. One Node. One Outage.
videoDescription:
Kubernetes replicas do not guarantee that your Pods run on different nodes. This animated example follows an API with three healthy replicas that all depend on one machine.

We reveal the shared node, inspect the Deployment's Pod template, and show how topology spread constraints guide the scheduler. The example uses node hostnames, maxSkew: 1, and DoNotSchedule across three eligible nodes.

A strict spreading rule can leave a Pod Pending when suitable capacity is unavailable. During the corrected replay, two replicas remain reachable after a node fails—but those surviving Pods still need enough headroom. Spreading across nodes is also different from spreading across zones.

Existing Pods do not move automatically when a spreading rule is added. The animation uses new Pod IDs for the changed rollout and labels the capacity example and replay separately.

#Kubernetes #DevOps #HighAvailability

videoDescription:

Chris Jia shares how she tamed delivery chaos as a company grew, by building a DevOps platform for a multi-stack enterprise. Isolated, on-demand environments, standardised delivery and self-service operations now support 20+ business units, 400 engineers and 500 applications.

videoTitle: PostgreSQL Databases Mastery: Deploy, Secure, Back Up and Recover a Real Database | Lesson 134
videoDescription:
Lesson 134 of the DevOps Engineering Bootcamp, and the mastery lesson of the Databases for DevOps domain. You prove everything together on one real PostgreSQL 16 server: fix and run a failing migration, create a least privilege role, fix the app's wrong port, take a backup with pg_dump, then survive an incident where a long idle transaction blocks the cart. You find the blocker with pg_stat_activity, end it with pg_terminate_backend, restore the backup into a new database and prove the data is back. A lab judges you from 0 of 6 to 6 of 6.

Chapters
0:00 Prove it all, in one scenario
0:26 What to expect
0:59 The whole domain in one map
1:47 The six missions
2:43 Live: the whole scenario, start to finish
8:29 Your lab task
8:59 Where to find the lab
10:07 Pass or fail rubric
10:35 Your turn
11:18 Quick check

Objectives covered: MC14-O01 to MC14-O08, the Databases for DevOps mastery evidence: complete an independently verifiable scenario, document results, troubleshooting and cleanup.

Get the lab: github.com/it-waves/devops-ai, in academy/lab (lab134.sh and shortcuts134.sh). Install with: sudo install -m 755 lab134.sh /usr/local/sbin/ then run lab up, lab check and lab down after loading the short names with: source shortcuts134.sh. You need any Linux machine with root, PostgreSQL server and client (for example: sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-client), and port 5514 free. The lab runs its own private PostgreSQL cluster in /opt/lab134 and does not touch the system PostgreSQL. lab down stops everything and removes it. Only run it on your own machine.

Honest notes: the terminal demo is one real, continuous recording of real PostgreSQL 16 and a small shell app and migration runner written for this lab, and the lab was run end to end: it passes 0 of 6 before you start and 6 of 6 after you finish, and lab down leaves nothing behind. The lab password sits in a plain text file only to keep the lesson simple: real teams use a secret manager. The narration is synthetic speech. The hook, map, missions, task, rubric and recap screens are labelled illustrations, not captures. Your own run is unverified until you do it.

Next lesson: Types of Software Tests: Unit, Integration, API, End-to-End, Smoke and Regression | Lesson 135 https://youtu.be/LHK5CDeXW_0

videoTitle: PostgreSQL Backup and Restore: pg_dump, pg_restore and Proving the Data | Lesson 130
videoDescription:
Lesson 130 of the DevOps Engineering Bootcamp, and lesson 5 of the Databases for DevOps domain. Someone runs DELETE FROM orders with no WHERE clause and every order is gone. A backup you never restored is only a hope. In this lesson you measure a real PostgreSQL 16 database, take a backup with pg_dump, check it is readable with pg_restore, cause the accident on purpose, restore into a new database instead of over production, and validate that the row count and the total match the numbers from before the disaster. You also learn recovery point and recovery time. A lab then judges you from 0 of 5 to 5 of 5.

Chapters
0:00 Back up. Break it. Restore it.
0:23 What to expect
0:58 Six ideas for backups that work
1:54 Live: back up, break it, restore, prove it
5:20 Your lab task
5:53 Where to find the lab
6:48 Pass or fail rubric
7:15 Your turn
7:53 Quick check
Objectives covered: MC14-O06 (back up and restore a database and validate recovered data)

Get the lab: github.com/it-waves/devops-ai, in academy/lab (lab130.sh and shortcuts130.sh). Install with: sudo install -m 755 lab130.sh /usr/local/sbin/ then run lab up, lab check and lab down after loading the short names with: source shortcuts130.sh. You need any Linux machine with root, PostgreSQL server and client (for example: sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-client) and port 5501 free. The lab runs its own private PostgreSQL cluster in /opt/lab130 and does not touch the system PostgreSQL. lab down stops it and removes everything. Only run it on your own machine.

Honest notes: the terminal part is one real, continuous recording on real PostgreSQL 16, and the lab was run end to end: it passes 0 of 5 before you start and 5 of 5 after you finish, and lab down leaves nothing behind. pg_dump makes a logical backup; very large databases often add physical backups and point-in-time recovery, which are beyond this lesson. The narration is synthetic speech. The hook, vocabulary, task, rubric and recap screens are labelled illustrations, not captures. Your own run is unverified until you do it.

videoTitle: What Happens When a Kubernetes Pod Crashes? #kubernetes
videoDescription:
Your pod just crashed. "It restarts" is only half the answer.

The kubelet restarts the container, based on the restart policy.
Keeps crashing? CrashLoopBackOff: it waits 10s, then 20s, then 40s, doubling up to 5 minutes.
Probes catch apps that hang: liveness restarts them, readiness pulls them out of traffic.

Follow for more.

videoTitle: Put nginx in Front of Tomcat: Reverse Proxy and HTTPS | Lesson 109
videoDescription:
Lesson 109 of the DevOps Engineering Bootcamp: put nginx in front of Tomcat. Tomcat answers in plain text on port 8084, so you add a reverse proxy that ends TLS. You make a self-signed certificate and key with openssl, write an nginx server block for HTTPS on port 8443 with proxy_pass to Tomcat, test it with nginx -t, and see why curl refuses the certificate without -k. Then you read the whoami page to see that Tomcat does not know the request was secure, add the X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For headers, and prove the app now sees them. A second server block on port 8085 redirects plain HTTP to HTTPS with a 301. In the same continuous screen recording, Chrome shows the "Your connection is not private" warning, the cart over HTTPS and the redirect.

Chapters
0:00 Why a reverse proxy
0:33 Four ideas
1:12 Live: certificate, proxy, headers, redirect
9:48 Your lab task
10:18 Where to find the lab
11:23 Pass or fail rubric
11:56 Your turn
12:34 Quick check

Objectives covered: MC12-O06 (a reverse proxy in front of Tomcat and TLS termination)

Get the lab: github.com/it-waves/devops-ai, in academy/lab (lab109.sh and shortcuts109.sh). Install with: sudo install -m 755 lab109.sh /usr/local/sbin/ then run lab up, lab check and lab down after loading the short names with: source shortcuts109.sh. You need any Linux machine with root, nginx, openssl, a JDK and curl (for example: sudo apt install -y nginx openssl openjdk-21-jdk-headless curl), internet access, about 1 GB of free memory and ports 8084, 8085 and 8443 free. No systemd is needed, and the lab runs its own nginx from the lab folder, so the system one is not touched. The first lab up downloads Tomcat 10.1.34 from archive.apache.org (about 14 MB). lab down stops both servers and removes everything. Only run it on your own machine.

videoTitle: A Service is private. So how do visitors get in? ⚓ #kubernetes #k8s #devops
videoDescription:
A Service is private by default. So how does a visitor from outside get in? ⚓

🚪 Through the gate: an Ingress, a list of rules for web traffic, matched on host and path.
🧭 shop.example.com/api goes to the API Service. Everything else goes to the web Service.
📄 But a rule is only paper. An Ingress controller reads it and does the routing. No controller, nothing happens.
🔐 It can also end TLS for you, so traffic inside is plain.
🆕 Gateway API is the newer option the Kubernetes project recommends. Ingress is frozen, with no plans to remove it.

Part 7 of Kubernetes in a minute.

videoTitle: Fix App-to-Database Connection Errors and Failed Migrations in PostgreSQL | Lesson 133
videoDescription:
Lesson 133 of the DevOps Engineering Bootcamp, and lesson 8 of the Databases for DevOps domain. Monday morning, the app is down: cannot connect to the database. In this lesson a real app fails four times in a row against a real PostgreSQL 16 server, and you fix one setting after each failure: the host name that does not resolve, the port with nothing listening (connection refused), the password that is rejected (password authentication failed), and the database name that does not exist. Then a schema migration fails halfway, and you see why it rolled back safely, fix the typo in the pending migration and rerun it. A lab then judges you from 0 of 5 to 5 of 5.

Chapters
0:00 Fix it, one layer at a time
0:28 What to expect
1:04 Eight ideas for a connection that fails
2:01 Live: fix the app, one layer at a time
6:54 Your lab task
7:24 Where to find the lab
8:20 Pass or fail rubric
8:41 Your turn
9:21 Quick check

Objectives covered: MC14-O08, troubleshoot app-to-database connectivity and migration failures.

Get the lab: github.com/it-waves/devops-ai, in academy/lab (lab133.sh and shortcuts133.sh). Install with: sudo install -m 755 lab133.sh /usr/local/sbin/ then run lab up, lab check and lab down after loading the short names with: source shortcuts133.sh. You need any Linux machine with root, PostgreSQL server and client (for example: sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-client), and port 5513 free. The lab runs its own private PostgreSQL cluster in /opt/lab133, with a deliberately broken app configuration and a failing migration, and does not touch the system PostgreSQL. lab down stops everything and removes it. Only run it on your own machine.

Honest notes: the terminal demo is one real, continuous recording of real PostgreSQL 16 and a small shell app and migration runner written for this lab, and the lab was run end to end: it passes 0 of 5 before you start and 5 of 5 after you finish, and lab down leaves nothing behind. The word-for-word error messages come from PostgreSQL 16 and may differ slightly in other versions. The lab password sits in a plain text file only to keep the lesson simple: real teams use a secret manager. The narration is synthetic speech. The hook, ideas, task, rubric and recap screens are labelled illustrations, not captures. Your own run is unverified until you do it.

videoTitle: What Is Progressive Delivery? Canary, Blue-Green and Feature Flags
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

What is progressive delivery? The umbrella over canary releases, blue-green deployments and feature flags, gradual rollouts that ship a change to a few users first, tested in a small model.

THE IDEA

Ship a new version to everyone, and if it is broken, everyone finds out. Progressive delivery ships to a few people first, lets a number judge it, and only then goes wider. Argo Rollouts defines it as releasing updates in a controlled and gradual manner, reducing the risk of the release.

THE MODEL

I built a small Python model to compare the tools. 1000 requests, and a new version that fails 1 request in 10.

      def handle(self, request):
          self.served += 1
          return self.served % 10 != 0

THE FIRST SURPRISE

Deploying code and releasing it to users are two different moves. Blue-green splits them with two identical environments. Blue serves everyone, green gets the new version with nobody on it. Test green, switch the router, and if anything breaks, switch it back. But the switch is all or nothing. In the model green passed a 5 request test, went live, and 100 of 1000 requests failed.

  green deployed, live requests on it: 0
  private test on green: 5 requests, 5 passed
  router to green: 1000 of 1000 requests
  failed: 100
  router back to blue: one change

THE CANARY

A canary sends a slice of real traffic to the new version and keeps the rest on the old one. The name comes from coal miners, whose caged canary met the gas before they did.

A NUMBER DECIDES, NOT A PERSON

In Argo Rollouts' own example, step one puts 20 percent of traffic on the canary, and a check reads its success rate. The example rule wants at least 0.95. The model's canary managed 0.90, so the check failed, the rollout aborted itself and the canary weight went back to zero. 20 requests failed, not 100.

        steps:
        - setWeight: 20
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
        - setWeight: 40
        - pause: {duration: 10m}

FEATURE FLAGS

A feature flag puts the switch inside the code. The new path ships turned off, so deploying it releases nothing. Turn it on for 10 percent of users, picked by user number, and each person always gets the same answer. In the model 10 requests failed, and turning the flag off put everyone back on the old path with no new deploy.

  def checkout(user_id, old, new):
      if flag_on("new-checkout", user_id):
          return new(user_id)
      return old(user_id)

  flag at 0%: 0 users on the new path
  flag at 10%: 100 of 1000 users on it
  failed: 10
  same users on a second pass: True
  flag at 0% again: 0 users, no deploy

WHERE YOUR SWITCH LIVES

Blue-green keeps it in the router and gives you the fastest way back. A canary keeps it in the traffic and lets a number stop a bad version. A flag keeps it in the code and picks exactly who sees it.

Never bet every user on one deploy. Show it to a few, let the numbers vote, then go wide.

videoTitle: MCP Explained for DevOps Engineers in 10 Minutes
videoDescription:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol in which an AI host's client calls tools on an MCP server. The model only proposes the call; it never executes it.
In 10 minutes, MCP explained for DevOps engineers, built as one diagram you can redraw from memory.

Subscribe for a new cloud and DevOps explainer every week: https://www.youtube.com/@InfraNarrative?sub_confirmation=1

What you'll learn:
- Host → client → server: each client holds exactly one connection to one server, and who actually runs your tool call
- The message sequence: initialize / tools/list / tools/call up to the November 2025 revision, and the stateless core in the July 28, 2026 revision
- stdio vs Streamable HTTP, when each is used, and how remote servers authenticate with OAuth 2.1
- A three-item safety checklist: scoped credentials, read-only by default, approval for write actions. Plus how to watch real messages in MCP Inspector

Spec revisions, flags and versions change. Everything here is as stated in the video. Check the current docs before relying on it.

videoTitle: Spec-Driven Development: The Complete Mental Model (Spec Kit, Kiro, OpenAPI & Pact)
videoDescription:
A one-line prompt can produce a beautiful dashboard — and quietly take down production. This audio deep dive builds a complete mental model of Spec-Driven Development (SDD): why vague "vibe coding" fails, how a reviewable spec drives planning and implementation, and how you verify the result against that spec rather than rewriting the spec to match the code.

Who it's for: beginners through interview level, especially DevOps, platform and software engineers working with AI coding agents, API contracts and multi-service systems. One running example throughout: an internal deploy-status API and dashboard.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:15 Why a one-line prompt can take down production
1:40 SDD is not a standard — the running example
4:13 The power inversion: code serves the spec
6:13 What SDD is, and why it isn't waterfall
9:00 Spec Kit workflow: constitution to implement
12:36 Quality gates: clarify, checklist, analyze
13:34 Converge: append-only verification
15:46 Contracts, schemas and idempotency
18:00 Persisting specs after delivery
19:07 Kiro: EARS, steering, hooks
22:35 Property-based tests and their limits
25:15 OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, TypeSpec
29:22 Pact and consumer-driven contract testing
32:19 BDD, pitfalls and the interview mental model
39:49 Outro

What it covers carefully: SDD is a named practice, not a standard (documented mainly by GitHub Spec Kit and, as a related product practice, Kiro). Current Spec Kit flow: constitution, then specify → plan → tasks → implement → converge, plus optional clarify, checklist and analyze gates. Converge is append-only. Kiro's requirements.md / design.md / tasks.md path, EARS, steering, hooks, and property-based tests (IDE-only, optional, evidence not formal proof). How OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, TypeSpec, JSON Schema, Pact and Cucumber BDD complement SDD without being SDD themselves.

Built from official GitHub Spec Kit, Kiro, OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, Pact and AWS/Microsoft documentationCorrection: at 18:23 the hosts mention three spec-persistence models; Spec Kit's docs list four, including Flow-forward.

videoTitle: PostgreSQL Basics: Connect with psql, Read the Schema, Run a Transaction | Lesson 126
videoDescription:
Lesson 126 of the DevOps Engineering Bootcamp, and lesson 1 of the Databases for DevOps domain. Your app is slow, shows an error, or lost an order, and nine times out of ten the answer is in the database. This lesson gives you the eight words you need (server, database, schema, table, row and column, connection, transaction, migration), then you use a real PostgreSQL 16 server: connect with psql, read the version, list and describe tables, count rows, read a migrations table, join three tables, check who is connected with pg_stat_activity, and run one transaction that rolls back and one that commits. A rolled-back row still uses up an id, and you see it happen. A lab then judges you from 0 of 5 to 5 of 5.

Chapters
0:00 Meet the database.
0:25 What to expect
1:02 Eight words to know
1:49 Live: connect, look, ask, change
7:06 Your lab task
7:34 Where to find the lab
8:30 Pass or fail rubric
8:50 Your turn
9:29 Quick check
Objectives covered: MC14-O01 (relational database, schema, connection, transaction, migration) and MC14-O02 (connect to PostgreSQL and run basic diagnostic SQL)

Get the lab: github.com/it-waves/devops-ai, in academy/lab (lab126.sh and shortcuts126.sh). Install with: sudo install -m 755 lab126.sh /usr/local/sbin/ then run lab up, lab check and lab down after loading the short names with: source shortcuts126.sh. You need any Linux machine with root, PostgreSQL server and client (for example: sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-client) and port 5461 free. The lab runs its own private PostgreSQL cluster in /opt/lab126 and does not touch the system PostgreSQL. lab down stops it and removes everything. Only run it on your own machine.

Honest notes: the terminal part is one real, continuous recording on real PostgreSQL 16, and the lab was run end to end: it passes 0 of 5 before you start and 5 of 5 after you finish, and lab down leaves nothing behind. The shop database is a tiny teaching example, so real databases are much bigger. The server is configured for local sockets with trust authentication in this lab only: never do that on a real server (we fix that in the next lesson). The narration is synthetic speech. The hook, vocabulary, task, rubric and recap screens are labelled illustrations, not captures. Your own run is unverified until you do it.

videoTitle: PostgreSQL Schema Migrations: Run, Fail, Fix and Repeat Safely | Lesson 129
videoDescription:
Lesson 129 of the DevOps Engineering Bootcamp, and lesson 4 of the Databases for DevOps domain. A Friday deploy expects a new column and the database does not have it: the site is down. Migrations fix this: small numbered SQL files, applied in order, recorded once in a schema_migrations table, each inside one transaction. In this lesson you run a real migration runner on a real PostgreSQL 16 server, watch migration 003 fail and roll back without leaving anything behind, fix it, run again so only the missing one applies, add your own migration 004, and prove that running the runner twice changes nothing. A lab then judges you from 0 of 5 to 5 of 5.

Chapters
0:00 Change the database safely
0:26 What to expect
1:04 Six ideas for safe migrations
1:58 Live: migrate, fail, fix, repeat
6:03 Your lab task
6:36 Where to find the lab
7:32 Pass or fail rubric
7:57 Your turn
8:33 Quick check
Objectives covered: MC14-O05 (run schema migrations in a deployment workflow)

Get the lab: github.com/it-waves/devops-ai, in academy/lab (lab129.sh and shortcuts129.sh). Install with: sudo install -m 755 lab129.sh /usr/local/sbin/ then run lab up, lab check and lab down after loading the short names with: source shortcuts129.sh. You need any Linux machine with root, PostgreSQL server and client (for example: sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-client) and port 5491 free. The lab runs its own private PostgreSQL cluster in /opt/lab129 and does not touch the system PostgreSQL. lab down stops it and removes everything. Only run it on your own machine.

Honest notes: the terminal part is one real, continuous recording on real PostgreSQL 16, and the lab was run end to end: it passes 0 of 5 before you start and 5 of 5 after you finish, and lab down leaves nothing behind. The runner is a tiny teaching script; real teams use tools such as Flyway, Liquibase or their framework's migrations, built on the same ideas. The narration is synthetic speech. The hook, vocabulary, task, rubric and recap screens are labelled illustrations, not captures. Your own run is unverified until you do it.

videoTitle: base64 isn't encryption: ConfigMaps and Secrets ⚓ #kubernetes #k8s #devops #shorts
videoDescription:
One image, running in dev and in production. But the settings differ, so don't bake them in. ⚓

🗒️ A ConfigMap holds plain settings as keys and values. Pods get them as environment variables or files.
🔑 A Secret holds passwords and tokens, used the same way.
👀 But the values are only base64. That's encoding, not encryption: anyone who can read the Secret can read the value.
🔒 By default, Secrets sit unencrypted in etcd. Turn on encryption at rest, and give out access sparingly.
♻️ Environment variables are read when the container starts, so changing them means restarting the pod.

Part 8 of Kubernetes in a minute.
